paragraphs: The purpose of acquiring and accumulating goods is conventionally held to be their consumption. This may be consumption directly by the owner, or by his household, which is identified with him in theory for this purpose. This is at least felt to be the economically legitimate end of acquisition, and the only one the theory is obliged to take into account. Such consumption may be seen as serving the consumer's physical wants, his physical comfort. It may also serve his so-called higher wants, whether spiritual, aesthetic or intellectual. These higher wants are served indirectly by spending goods, in a way familiar to all readers of economics.

Yet consumption can be said to provide the incentive behind accumulation only in a sense far removed from its naive meaning. The motive that lies at the root of ownership is emulation, the desire to outdo others. This same motive remains active as the institution it created develops further. It also shapes every feature of the social structure that the institution of ownership touches. The possession of wealth confers honour; it is an invidious distinction, one that sets a person above others. Nothing equally convincing can be said for consumption, nor for any other possible incentive to acquire goods, and least of all for accumulating wealth.

Of course, one fact must not be overlooked. Where nearly all goods are private property, the need to earn a living is a powerful and ever present incentive for the poorer members. Some classes are habitually employed at manual labour, live on a precarious footing, possess little and usually accumulate little. For them, the need for subsistence and greater physical comfort may for a time be the dominant motive. But the discussion will show that even among these poor classes, the weight of physical want is not as decisive as has sometimes been assumed.

On the other hand, consider the members and classes of the community who are chiefly concerned with accumulating wealth. For them, the incentive of subsistence or physical comfort never plays a significant part. Ownership began and grew into a human institution for reasons unrelated to the minimum needed to survive. From the outset, the dominant incentive was the invidious distinction attached to wealth. Except temporarily and by exception, no other motive has taken its place at any later stage of development.

Property began as booty held as trophies of a successful raid. As long as the group stayed in close contact with other hostile groups, the usefulness of owned things or persons lay chiefly in an invidious comparison. This comparison was between their possessor and the enemy from whom they had been taken. The habit of distinguishing the interests of the individual from those of his group apparently developed later. No doubt there was also an early comparison between the owner of the honorific booty and his less successful neighbours within the group. This added to the usefulness of the things possessed, though at first it was not the main element of their value. A man's prowess was still primarily the group's prowess. The possessor of the booty felt himself to be primarily the keeper of his group's honour. This communal view of great deeds also appears later, especially with the laurels of war.
